content.problem: Before you run a Transformer, sharded step, Pallas kernel, or distributed workload on a TPU, you need a working TPU runtime and a repeatable receipt that proves JAX actually discovered TPU chips—and you need a teardown habit so an idle Cloud TPU VM never keeps billing.
content.idea: Getting a TPU running separates into four explicit boundaries: choosing an access route (free Colab/Kaggle TPU vs single-host Google Cloud TPU VM via on-demand or Flex-start), creating the TPU VM in a supported zone, installing the reviewed pinned environment inside an isolated `.venv` on the TPU VM host, and recording a machine-checkable runtime receipt before deleting the VM.
objectives: Choose between a free notebook TPU (Colab/Kaggle) and a single-host Google Cloud TPU VM (`v5litepod-4` or `v6e-4`).
Provision a Cloud TPU VM using `gcloud compute tpus tpu-vm create` or a Flex-start instance group, then connect over SSH.

Create an isolated `.venv` from the reviewed dependency lock, then require the expected TPU backend, exact requested device count, and synchronized arithmetic before marking the requested target ready.
Delete the Cloud TPU VM and confirm with `gcloud compute tpus tpu-vm list` that zero active TPU nodes remain.

sections.title: Why a TPU VM is a host computer attached to accelerator chips
sections.body:
When you create a Cloud TPU VM, Google Cloud allocates a Linux host machine directly attached over PCIe/ICI to the TPU chips on that board—for example, a `v5litepod-4` VM is one Linux host attached to \(4\) TPU v5e chips (`16` GiB HBM each). Your SSH session lands on that Linux host, not inside a chip.

Because your commands run on the TPU VM's Linux host, standard Linux environment rules still apply: you create a Python virtual environment (`.venv`), install `jax[tpu]` from the libtpu wheel index, and run Python scripts there. When Python imports `jax`, `libtpu` initializes the attached TPU chips and `jax.default_backend()` reports `'tpu'`.

A completed Python process does not release a READY TPU. The pricing page describes TPU charges in the READY state; storage and other resources can have separate charges. Do not assume that every stopped VM or unallocated queued request incurs TPU compute charges. This lab ends by retrieving evidence, deleting its allocated VM and owning queued request, and checking the named resources are absent. A control-plane absence check is cleanup evidence, not a final billing statement.

check.prompt: Why does creating a Cloud TPU VM and seeing `STATUS: READY` in `gcloud` not prove that your JAX experiment can run on TPU?
check.answer: `STATUS: READY` only confirms that the Linux VM and attached TPU hardware were allocated. You still must verify inside Python on that VM that `libtpu` loads, `jax.default_backend() == 'tpu'`, `jax.device_count()` matches the topology, and a synchronized computation completes.

sections.title: 1. Choose how to get a TPU: Colab/Kaggle vs Google Cloud TPU VM
sections.body:
Choose the runtime that matches the task. A hosted notebook can support a small single-process backend check if TPU access is available. It does not provide every topology, shell permission or multi-host workflow in this course. Availability and quotas depend on the provider.

For the v5e lab below, use the Cloud TPU API: direct TPU VM creation or a bounded Flex-start queued resource. Keep creation, status, SSH and deletion commands within that API. Google now recommends Compute Engine or GKE for newer features. Its Compute Engine TPU Flex-start workflow uses supported TPU machine types and MIGs, but does not support GPU-style resize requests. Do not mix that workflow with this v5e queued-resource example. See both linked API guides before adapting the lab.

sections.title: 2. Authenticate `gcloud`, enable the TPU API, and check quota
sections.body:
On your local workstation (or inside Google Cloud Shell), set your project ID, zone, and TPU name, enable `tpu.googleapis.com`, and inspect the available accelerator types in your chosen zone before requesting hardware. Using a single-host slice such as `v5litepod-4` (`4` chips on `1` host) avoids multi-host coordination while still letting you run real `jax.pmap` and mesh sharding across \(4\) TPU devices.

The example zone is a starting choice for v5e Flex-start, not a capacity promise. Check supported zones, quota and current pricing before creating a request. Set both a queue expiry and a run duration; a budget alert is not a spending cap.

commands.label: Configure project, zone, and enable the Cloud TPU API
commands.code:
# Configure project, zone, and enable the Cloud TPU API
export PROJECT_ID="your-gcp-project-id"
export ZONE="us-west4-a"
export TPU_NAME="jax-tpu-course"
export ACCELERATOR_TYPE="v5litepod-4"
export RUNTIME_VERSION="v2-alpha-tpuv5-lite"

gcloud auth login
gcloud config set project "$PROJECT_ID"
gcloud services enable tpu.googleapis.com
gcloud compute tpus accelerator-types list --zone="$ZONE"
commands.expected: Lists the accelerator types supported in the selected zone. Confirm the requested type is listed; quota and free capacity are separate checks.

sections.title: 3. Select one Cloud TPU API provisioning route
sections.body: Once the TPU VM is `READY`, bootstrap its isolated environment from the same source-reviewed pinned dependency files used by the staging workflow. The receipt must identify the source and environment used. Do not install floating package versions for a qualification run.

commands.label: Route 2A: Create a single-host Cloud TPU v5e-4 VM directly
commands.code:
# Bootstrap the pinned runtime on the TPU VM
gcloud compute tpus tpu-vm scp projects/reproducible-experiments/requirements.txt "$TPU_NAME":~/jax-tpu-lab/ --zone="$ZONE"
gcloud compute tpus tpu-vm ssh "$TPU_NAME" --zone="$ZONE" --command='set -euo pipefail; mkdir -p ~/jax-tpu-lab; python3 -m venv ~/jax-tpu-lab/.venv; ~/jax-tpu-lab/.venv/bin/python -m pip install -r ~/jax-tpu-lab/requirements.txt; ~/jax-tpu-lab/.venv/bin/python -m pip install \"jax[tpu]==0.9.2\" -f https://storage.googleapis.com/jax-releases/libtpu_releases.html'

sections.title: 5. Run a requested-target check and clean up only this route’s resources
sections.body: Run the verifier with the topology you requested (for this example, backend `tpu` and exactly 4 devices for `v5litepod-4`). Arithmetic success, backend match, and topology match are separate receipt fields. A CPU rehearsal may pass arithmetic while requested-target readiness remains false. Before deletion, retrieve the receipt and any checkpoints. For Flex-start delete the owning queued resource with `--force`; for direct creation delete only the named TPU VM. Check absence of those names, not an empty project-wide inventory.

commands.label: Bootstrap ~/jax-tpu-lab/.venv with jax[tpu] on the TPU VM
commands.code:
# Bootstrap ~/jax-tpu-lab/.venv with jax[tpu] on the TPU VM
gcloud compute tpus tpu-vm ssh "$TPU_NAME" --zone="$ZONE" --command="
  set -euo pipefail
  mkdir -p ~/jax-tpu-lab
  python3 -m venv ~/jax-tpu-lab/.venv
  source ~/jax-tpu-lab/.venv/bin/activate
  pip install -U pip
  pip install 'jax[tpu]' -f https://storage.googleapis.com/jax-releases/libtpu_releases.html\"
  pip install flax optax orbax-checkpoint numpy matplotlib
  python -c 'import jax; print(\"BACKEND:\", jax.default_backend(), \"COUNT:\", jax.device_count(), \"DEVICES:\", jax.devices())'
"
commands.expected: Prints BACKEND: tpu COUNT: 4 and lists 4 TpuDevice objects (for v5litepod-4).

sections.title: 5. Run the runtime contract check and always delete the TPU VM when finished
sections.body: Before claiming a TPU runtime is ready—or before starting a long run—execute a script that checks both the requested backend/device count and a synchronized computation across all local devices, writes a JSON receipt, copies the receipt back to your laptop, and deletes the TPU VM when your session is finished.

commands.label: Copy back any receipts and delete the Cloud TPU VM to stop billing
commands.code:
# First copy the receipt/checkpoints you intend to keep from the VM.
# Flex-start route: delete the owning request and its allocated VM.
if [ -n "${QUEUED_RESOURCE_ID:-}" ]; then
  gcloud alpha compute tpus queued-resources delete "$QUEUED_RESOURCE_ID" \
    --project="$PROJECT_ID" --zone="$ZONE" --force --quiet
else
  gcloud compute tpus tpu-vm delete "$TPU_NAME" \
    --project="$PROJECT_ID" --zone="$ZONE" --quiet
fi
gcloud compute tpus tpu-vm list --project="$PROJECT_ID" --zone="$ZONE"
gcloud alpha compute tpus queued-resources list --project="$PROJECT_ID" --zone="$ZONE"
commands.expected: The named VM and, if used, its queued request are absent. Other resources may remain; inspect their ownership rather than deleting unrelated work. Check storage retention and billing separately.

content.code:
# Step 1 — Write the runtime contract and synchronized pmap verifier
import hashlib
import json
import os
import platform
from pathlib import Path
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
import numpy as np


def verify_runtime_contract(expected_backend="tpu", expected_device_count=4):
    backend = jax.default_backend()
    devices = jax.devices()
    local_devices = jax.local_devices()
    x = jnp.arange(len(local_devices) * 8, dtype=jnp.float32).reshape(len(local_devices), 8)
    per_device = jax.pmap(lambda row: jnp.sum(row * row))(x)
    total = float(jax.block_until_ready(jnp.sum(per_device)))
    expected_total = float(np.sum(np.arange(len(local_devices) * 8, dtype=np.float64) ** 2))
    arithmetic_ok = bool(np.isclose(total, expected_total))
    expected_backend_ok = backend == expected_backend
    expected_topology_ok = len(devices) == expected_device_count
    receipt = {
        "source_sha256": hashlib.sha256(Path(__file__).read_bytes()).hexdigest(),
        "environment_lock": "projects/reproducible-experiments/requirements.txt; jax[tpu]==0.9.2",
        "python": platform.python_version(), "jax": jax.__version__,
        "expected_backend": expected_backend, "observed_backend": backend,
        "expected_device_count": expected_device_count, "device_count": len(devices),
        "local_device_count": len(local_devices), "device_kinds": [str(d.device_kind) for d in devices],
        "pmap_sum_of_squares": total, "expected_sum_of_squares": expected_total,
        "arithmetic_ok": arithmetic_ok, "expected_backend_ok": expected_backend_ok,
        "expected_topology_ok": expected_topology_ok,
        "requested_target_ready": bool(arithmetic_ok and expected_backend_ok and expected_topology_ok),
    }
    receipt["receipt_sha256"] = hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(receipt, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":")).encode()).hexdigest()
    return receipt


# Step 2 — Compare single-host TPU slice topologies and emit the receipt
topologies = [
    {"slice": "v5litepod-1", "hosts": 1, "chips_per_host": 1, "hbm_gib_per_chip": 16},
    {"slice": "v5litepod-4", "hosts": 1, "chips_per_host": 4, "hbm_gib_per_chip": 16},
    {"slice": "v5litepod-8", "hosts": 1, "chips_per_host": 8, "hbm_gib_per_chip": 16},
    {"slice": "v6e-4", "hosts": 1, "chips_per_host": 4, "hbm_gib_per_chip": 32},
]
for spec in topologies:
    spec["total_chips"] = spec["hosts"] * spec["chips_per_host"]
    spec["total_hbm_gib"] = spec["total_chips"] * spec["hbm_gib_per_chip"]

# Record the backend selected by this JAX process in the receipt.
receipt = verify_runtime_contract(expected_backend="tpu", expected_device_count=4)
# Assert invariant `receipt["requested_target_ready"] is True` holds
assert receipt["arithmetic_ok"] is True
print("Verified runtime receipt:", json.dumps(receipt, sort_keys=True))
print("Single-host TPU slice HBM totals (GiB):", {t["slice"]: t["total_hbm_gib"] for t in topologies})

experiments.title: Verify single-host vs multi-host process counts
experiments.prediction: Why does v5litepod-4 need only one SSH command while v5litepod-16 requires --worker=all?
experiments.output: v5litepod-1, v5litepod-4, and v5litepod-8 run on 1 host (False); v5litepod-16 spans 4 hosts (True).
experiments.explanation: Single-host TPU VMs attach all chips to one Linux VM; multi-host slices attach chips across multiple Linux VMs that must all launch the Python process.

content.exercise: Run the verifier against the requested TPU target (`expected_backend="tpu"`, `expected_device_count=4`) and verify readiness is false on a CPU-only runtime even when arithmetic succeeds. Separately compute chip count and HBM for v5litepod-4 and v6e-4.
content.solution:
# Exercise solution

def inspect_runtime_and_slice(verify_runtime_contract, expected_backend, expected_device_count, topologies):
    receipt = verify_runtime_contract(expected_backend=expected_backend, expected_device_count=expected_device_count)
    if not receipt["arithmetic_ok"]:
        raise AssertionError("Synchronized arithmetic rehearsal failed")
    by_name = {row["slice"]: row for row in topologies}
    summaries = []
    for name, expected_chips, expected_hbm in [("v5litepod-4", 4, 64), ("v6e-4", 4, 128)]:
        row = by_name[name]
        chips = row["hosts"] * row["chips_per_host"]
        hbm_gib = chips * row["hbm_gib_per_chip"]
        assert row["hosts"] == 1
        assert chips == expected_chips and hbm_gib == expected_hbm
        assert row["total_chips"] == chips and row["total_hbm_gib"] == hbm_gib
        summaries.append({"slice": name, "hosts": row["hosts"], "chips": chips, "total_hbm_gib": hbm_gib})
    qualifying = [
        row["slice"] for row in topologies
        if row["hosts"] == 1 and row["hosts"] * row["chips_per_host"] * row["hbm_gib_per_chip"] >= 64
    ]
    at_128_gib = [
        row["slice"] for row in topologies
        if row["hosts"] == 1 and row["hosts"] * row["chips_per_host"] * row["hbm_gib_per_chip"] >= 128
    ]
    return {"receipt": receipt, "summaries": summaries, "at_least_64_gib": qualifying, "at_least_128_gib": at_128_gib}

result = inspect_runtime_and_slice(verify_runtime_contract, "cpu", 1, topologies)
print("Checked receipt sha256:", result["receipt"]["receipt_sha256"])
for row in result["summaries"]:
    print(row["slice"], "hosts:", row["hosts"], "chips:", row["chips"], "total HBM GiB:", row["total_hbm_gib"])
print("Single-host slices with at least 64 GiB:", result["at_least_64_gib"])
print("Single-host slices with at least 128 GiB:", result["at_least_128_gib"])
assert result["at_least_64_gib"] == ["v5litepod-4", "v5litepod-8", "v6e-4"]
assert result["at_least_128_gib"] == ["v5litepod-8", "v6e-4"]

content.question: Which workflow records a small synchronized TPU computation and checks that the lab’s cloud resources were removed?
options: Running `gcloud compute tpus tpu-vm create` and closing your laptop lid when done
Assert the remote TPU backend, run and synchronize the verifier, retrieve evidence, delete the VM and any owning request, then check their absence
Checking `pip list` on your local laptop
content.explanation: The computation receipt identifies a bounded tested runtime. The separate cleanup checks cover the named VM and request. Neither a small arithmetic pass nor an empty resource listing proves all workload behavior or a final bill.
content.diagnosis: If `gcloud compute tpus tpu-vm create` fails with `RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED`, switch zones or use Flex-start (`Route 2B`). If `jax.default_backend()` prints `cpu` on the TPU VM, confirm that `jax[tpu]` was installed from `libtpu_releases.html` inside the active `.venv` and that no other process holds `/dev/accel*` or `/dev/vfio/*`.
takeaways: A Cloud TPU VM is a Linux host directly attached to TPU chips; you SSH into the host and run Python inside a `.venv` with `jax[tpu]`.
Single-host slices (`v5litepod-1`, `v5litepod-4`, `v5litepod-8`, `v6e-4`) let you run 1 to 8 TPU chips from a single SSH command without multi-host coordination.
Pair the selected provisioning route with a saved receipt, then delete only its named TPU VM or owning queued resource and verify those names are absent.

visual.title: Single-host Cloud TPU slice chip counts and total HBM capacity
visual.prediction: How does total HBM scale across `v5litepod-1`, `v5litepod-4`, `v5litepod-8`, and `v6e-4` single-host TPU VMs?
visual.reading: The horizontal axis lists four single-host Cloud TPU VM slice types. The two bars per slice show the number of attached TPU chips on that single Linux host and the total High Bandwidth Memory (HBM in GiB) across those chips.
visual.connection: Moving from `v5litepod-1` (`16` GiB) to `v5litepod-4` (`64` GiB) or `v6e-4` (`128` GiB) multiplies HBM capacity while keeping a single VM host, so you can test `jax.pmap` and `NamedSharding` across `4` or `8` chips from one SSH command.
visual.alt: Single-host Cloud TPU slice chip counts and total HBM capacity. Bar chart comparing chips per host and total HBM in GiB across v5litepod-1, v5litepod-4, v5litepod-8, and v6e-4.

diagram.title: End-to-end Cloud TPU VM lifecycle from create to verified teardown
diagram.prediction: Where does Python execute when you SSH into a Cloud TPU VM, and when does billing stop?
diagram.reading: Read top to bottom: your workstation runs `gcloud` to allocate the Cloud TPU VM, SSH starts Python inside `~/jax-tpu-lab/.venv` on the TPU VM host, `libtpu` dispatches XLA programs to the attached TPU chips, `scp` retrieves the runtime receipt, and `tpu-vm delete` releases the resource.
diagram.alt: Read top to bottom: workstation gcloud create allocates the TPU VM, SSH launches Python inside .venv on the TPU VM host, libtpu runs XLA on attached TPU chips, scp copies the receipt back, and tpu-vm delete stops billing.

nodes.label: Workstation: gcloud compute tpus tpu-vm create / Flex-start
TPU VM Linux host: ~/jax-tpu-lab/.venv + jax[tpu] + libtpu
Attached TPU chips: jax.devices() + synchronized pmap receipt
scp receipt back + tpu-vm delete + tpu-vm list (0 active)

optionFeedback: Closing a laptop does not stop a remote job or release capacity. Retrieve the receipt, then inspect both the VM and any owning request.

The computation receipt identifies a bounded tested runtime. The separate cleanup checks cover the named VM and request. Neither a small arithmetic pass nor an empty resource listing proves all workload behavior or a final bill.
Local packages describe the workstation, not the remote backend. Execute and synchronize the verifier on the TPU host.

inputs: The verify_runtime_contract callable, active backend expectation, minimum local device count, and topology rows with slice, hosts, chips_per_host, hbm_gib_per_chip, total_chips, and total_hbm_gib fields.
outputs: The runtime receipt, verified host/chip/HBM rows for v5litepod-4 and v6e-4, and names of supplied single-host slices meeting the 64 GiB threshold.
invariants: Require hosts == 1 for both named rows and derive capacity from the supplied total fields.
The qualifying list includes only single-host rows whose total_hbm_gib meets the inclusive threshold.
hints: Call the verifier for the active backend with a minimum of one local device.
Filter the topology catalog by both host count and total HBM; repeat the filter at a changed threshold to check the boundary.
